In Hebrew of the Old Testament, it often translates תַּחְתּוֹן (tachton) or תַּחְתִּי (tachtî), which have the same idea: what is below, what belongs to the lower regions.
G2737.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament: in Ephesians 4:9. Paul uses it to describe Christ's descent after his resurrection. The expression "lower regions of the earth" (or "lower parts of the earth") was a way of speaking about the abode of the dead, consistent with the biblical vision of the cosmos where the earth also encompasses the subterranean depths. This passage has been variously interpreted by the Church Fathers, but the context of the Epistle to the Ephesians emphasizes Christ's descent and ascent as stages of his exaltation.
G2737.portee: This word helps to understand biblical cosmology: for the authors of the New Testament, the physical world has a vertical structure — high and low — and this cosmic geography is not mere physics, but the framework in which Christ's power is exercised. Meditating on this descent of Christ to the "lower regions" enriches the confession of his universal lordship.

sens: High temperature, fervor of the sun or fire
Physical suffering caused by the burning of fire or the sun
Divine torment, heavenly punishment
G2738.detail:
1. Heat is primarily simply intense temperature: that of the sun beating down mercilessly, or that of fire. In Revelation 7:16, the blessed in heaven will no longer suffer from this burning heat of the sun — which evokes the contrast with the earth where heat exhausts and wounds. It is the biblical image of the arid desert, of elemental physical suffering.
2. Heat becomes suffering when it burns: in Revelation 16:9, people are literally burned by a great heat, a physical torment. It is not merely uncomfortable: it is a scourge, a plague that causes intense suffering.
3. This burning heat is also a symbol of divine punishment. It does not come by chance: it is the weapon of God's judgment, and those who endure it recognize (or should recognize) that it comes from God. That is why the people in Revelation 16:9 blaspheme the name of God: they know that this heat is his judgment.
G2738.origine: The Greek word kauma comes from the verb kaïō which means to burn, to make fire. It is a common, direct derivative: heat is literally what one feels when something burns. In the Greek Bible, this word translates the Hebrew hom (חֹם) or horeb (חֹרֶב), which similarly denote intense heat, often that of the sun or the desert.
G2738.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both times in Revelation, the last prophetic book. In Revelation 7:16, it first describes the comfort of the elect in heaven: they are spared from hunger, thirst, and the heat of the sun. It is a vision of peace and rest. In Revelation 16:9, the same heat returns, but inverted: it is now one of the divine plagues that burns the people of the earth, provoking not repentance but blasphemy. Heat is thus alternately the symbol of earthly suffering from which the elect will be delivered, and of divine judgment that will strike the unrepentant.
G2738.portee: This word reminds that the faithful will inherit a world without physical suffering: no more burning heat, hunger, thirst. But it also warns that God's judgment manifests through concrete realities — not abstract ones — and that rejecting God in the face of his acts leads only to blasphemy, never to true repentance. The heat of the blessed heaven is a promise; the heat of judgment, a warning.

sens: To be consumed by fire or intense heat
To dry up and wither under the effect of heat
To be affected or damaged by a burn
G2739.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical: to be consumed by fire or extreme heat that destroys. In Revelation 16:8-9, during the plagues of the end times, the sun literally burns men with such intense heat that it torments them.

2. In the parable of the sower (Matthew 13:6 and Mark 4:6), the young plant is burned — dried up and dead — by the day's sun because it has no deep roots to draw moisture from the soil. This is an image of what withers quickly, lacking depth.

3. The word emphasizes the idea of destruction or suffering caused by devastating heat or fire, whether literal or metaphorical.
G2739.origine: The word comes from the root « καῦμα » which means heat or burn. It expresses the action of being burned or heated to the extreme. The family of this Greek word always conveys the idea of destructive heat and consumption.
G2739.emploi: The word appears four times in total in the New Testament, always in the passive voice (that is, it is the one who is burned who undergoes the action). Twice in the parable of the sower in Matthew and Mark, where the rootless plant is burned by the sun and cannot grow. Twice in Revelation, chapter 16, where it describes the final plagues: the sun burns men with terrible heat. The meaning remains constant: destruction by heat or fire.
G2739.portee: This biblical image of burning speaks to us about the fragility of what lacks a solid foundation. The young plant burned without roots symbolizes superficial conversions that do not withstand trials. For the Christian, it invites us to root ourselves deeply in faith. The apocalyptic visions also show the consequences of rejecting God: terrible suffering for those who turn away from Him.

sens: The action or state of burning, consuming by flames
Destruction or condemnation by fire
G2740.detail:
1. The word designates the act of burning, the process by which fire consumes something. In Hebrews 6:8, Paul speaks of a land that produces thorns and thistles: "it is eventually burned" — this is the concrete action of fire, which destroys what is useless.
2. By extension, fire becomes the image of destruction and divine judgment: the rejected land deserves to be consumed, reflecting its spiritual condemnation.
G2740.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb καίω (kaïô), "to burn," which describes the action of fire. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, it often translates בָּעַר (ba'ar) in the intensive form, which also means "to burn, consume." The root evokes the fundamental image of fire that destroys and purifies.
G2740.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 6:8. Paul uses it to describe the fate of a land that bears useless fruit (thorns and thistles): it is "rejected and near to being cursed" and ends up being consumed by fire. The context is a parable of divine judgment: just as a barren or bad land is destroyed by fire, so one who refuses to produce spiritual fruit exposes themselves to condemnation.
G2740.portee: This word reminds us that the refusal to produce fruit in the Christian life is not without consequences. Fire symbolizes here divine judgment, not an arbitrary threat, but God's just reaction to unfaithfulness. For the believer, it is a call to remain spiritually productive, rooted in the grace received.

sens: Consumed, destroyed by fire
Burning with intense heat
G2741.detail:
1. The word describes something that is consumed or destroyed by fire with great intensity. In 2 Peter 3:10, the apostle Peter speaks of the "burned elements" that "will be dissolved" on the day of the Lord — an image of total cosmic destruction, where even the material components of the world will be reduced to nothing by extreme heat.
2. More broadly, the term evokes a burning and devouring heat. In 2 Peter 3:12, the "burned elements" that "will melt" reinforce this idea: it is a fire so violent that it melts matter itself, like molten metal.
G2741.origine: The word comes from a Greek root expressing burning heat and fever (καῦσος, kaûsos). The passive form found here — "to be burned" — suggests an action undergone, a destruction by an external power. It is a rare word, used mainly to speak of phenomena of intense heat or combustion.
G2741.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the New Testament, solely in the two verses of 2 Peter 3 concerning the events of the end times. The apostle uses it to describe the dissolution of the material cosmos on the day of judgment: the elements of the physical world will be burned and destroyed. This apocalyptic context gives the word its gravity and prophetic weight — it is not an ordinary image of fire, but the image of the final destruction of the current creation.
G2741.portee: This word reminds us that the Lord will judge not only men but also the material creation itself. It invites us not to place our trust in the perishable things of this world, but to await the coming of Christ and the new creation that God will establish. It is a call to vigilance and hope.

sens: The intense and burning heat of the sun
A hot and drying wind coming from the east
The heatwave or the scorching midday sun
G2742.detail:
1. The intense heat of the sun: it is the burning sensation produced by the sun at its zenith. In Matthew 20:12, the workers who have worked all day complain of having "endured the fatigue of the day and the heat," referring to this physical oppression under the midday sun.
2. A hot, drying wind: in the Mediterranean, it is the sirocco, this dry and suffocating wind that blows from the east and south. Luke 12:55 shows Jesus teaching to recognize the signs: when "the south wind blows," "it will be hot," and this burning wind indeed arrives.
3. The destructive effect of this extreme heat: James 1:11 describes how the sun "rose with its scorching heat," it dried up the grass and caused its flower to fall. This is the classic biblical image of a force that exhausts, destroys, and reminds us of the fragility of all that is earthly.
G2742.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb meaning "to burn" or "to inflame." It translates in the Old Testament words like the "east wind" (קָדִים, qâdîm), which in the Bible refers to the hot desert wind known for its destructive power (see Ezekiel 17:10, where this wind dries up the vines). It is a concrete term, derived from a climatic reality well known to Mediterraneans and inhabitants of the Near East.
G2742.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament, always to describe an external and hostile heat. In Matthew 20:12 and Luke 12:55, it is the heat of the day and the south wind, everyday realities that people know well. James 1:11 makes it a symbol of destruction: the heat of the sun burns the grass and the flower, a powerful image of the vanity of earthly riches and human fragility in the face of the forces of time. In these three contexts, it is a real physical force, not an abstraction.
G2742.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible speaks the language of the men and women of this world: it knows the pain of working under the burning sun, the fatigue of the body, and the wear of time. The image of heat that dries and destroys, in James, invites the reader not to cling to passing riches, but to seek what endures. For those who suffer, this word also says that the Bible recognizes this physical suffering.

sens: To burn or mark the skin with a hot instrument, as was once done to cattle or slaves
Figuratively, to destroy moral sensitivity, making the conscience insensitive to guilt
G2743.detail: 1. The verb literally refers to the action of marking something or someone by burning with a heated iron. It is the image of a seal or mark left on the skin, as was done to animals for identification. 2. The Bible uses it figuratively to describe a 'seared' conscience or one that has become insensitive to sin. In 1 Timothy 4:2, Paul speaks of those whose conscience is 'seared with a hot iron' by their own religious lies: they have so suppressed the voice of God within them that they no longer feel guilt, as if their heart has become a scarred wound, incapable of feeling.
G2743.origine: The word comes from καυτήριον, which refers to the branding iron, the instrument used for marking by fire. It is derived from the root καίω (to burn). The image is that of an indelible mark left by heat — a seal engraved in the flesh. By transferring this image to the conscience, the verb suggests a moral wound that has healed over, an insensitivity acquired through the habit of sin.
G2743.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Timothy 4:2, where Paul uses it in the past participle to describe the spiritual state of certain false teachers. Their conscience is 'seared with a hot iron' — meaning it has lost its natural ability to discern right from wrong, rendered mute by repeated lies and hypocrisy. The passive and perfect usage emphasizes that this scarring is complete, representing the present and lasting state of these men.
G2743.portee: This word warns Christians about a serious spiritual danger: the habit of sin and lies eventually extinguishes the voice of the conscience. It is a call not to harden one's heart against the truth of God, for a 'seared' conscience loses its warning ability and becomes complicit in our own lies.

sens: To brag, to take pride in something
To take pride in one's merits, achievements, or status
To exult in something beneficial or worthy
To place one's trust and honor in God or Christ rather than in oneself
G2744.detail:
1. To boast or to glorify oneself means to speak proudly of oneself or what one possesses, seeking the approval of others. This can be innocent: Paul boasts of the conversions he has led (2 Corinthians 10:15), or condemnable: some 'boast according to the flesh' claiming a carnal superiority (2 Corinthians 11:18).
2. It also means to draw honor or prestige from one's position, talents, or personal merit. For example, to boast of possessing the law or the name of Jew (Romans 2:17) amounts to believing oneself spiritually superior.
3. But the Bible also speaks of a joyful and healthy exultation — rejoicing in good news without selfish pride: believers boast in the hope of salvation in Christ (Romans 5:3, 5:11).
4. The noblest use of the word is to 'boast in God' or 'in Christ' (Romans 2:17; 1 Corinthians 1:31): this means placing all one's pride, trust, and joy in God alone, recognizing that all that is good comes from Him. Paul rejoices in this: 'Therefore I will boast all the more gladly of my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may rest upon me' (2 Corinthians 12:9).
G2744.origine: The Greek verb καυχάομαι comes from a root expressing the idea of showing oneself, displaying, or taking pride. In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew verb הָלַל (hallal), which means 'to celebrate', 'to praise', 'to boast'. The Hebrew root suggests the idea of making noise, proclaiming aloud — hence the shift from the meaning of 'praising God' (positive use) to 'boasting of oneself' (negative use). The word family includes forms with prefixes (κατακαυχάομαι, 'to despise while boasting'), showing how this sentiment can manifest in different forms.
G2744.emploi: This verb appears 33 times in the New Testament, mostly in Paul’s writings (Romans, 1-2 Corinthians, Galatians) and in the epistle of James. Paul uses it primarily in two contexts: first, he denounces carnal boasting — false glory derived from the law, status, or appearances (Romans 2:17, 2:23) — and asserts that 'no flesh should boast in the presence of God' (1 Corinthians 1:29). Secondly, he teaches legitimate glory: one should 'boast in God' or 'in the Lord' (Romans 5:11; 1 Corinthians 1:31), which includes exultation in tribulations (Romans 5:3) or in signs of apostleship (2 Corinthians 10:15, 10:17). An important nuance: Paul even accepts 'boasting' in his weakness or personal weaknesses (2 Corinthians 12:5, 12:9), for they reveal the power of Christ. James also warns against boasting (James 4:16), while praising the poor who boast in their Christian exaltation (James 1:9).
G2744.portee: This word invites the believer to crucial discernment: it is not forbidden to rejoice or recognize what is good in oneself, but all legitimate glory must find its source in God and Christ, not in oneself. To boast in weaknesses rather than strengths is to learn to let God act and to renounce the desire to appear. For the Christian, the issue is spiritual: where does he place his identity, pride, and hope? In Christ alone, or in himself and in what is visible?

sens: That which one boasts about, reason or cause for pride
Honor or reputation resulting from it
Reason to boast or matter for exaltation
Title of pride shared with others
G2745.detail:
1. It is primarily simply the thing or fact that someone boasts about — what deserves or seems to deserve pride. It is the concrete motive for boasting: Paul asks 'do I have a subject of glory?' in 1 Corinthians 9:15, meaning a valid reason to boast about proclaiming the Gospel.
2. It is also the honor or reputation derived from it, the luster gained by this motive. The Corinthians boast 'wrongly' about a shameful matter (1 Corinthians 5:6): they derive false glory from a situation that should humiliate them.
3. By extension, it is simply the matter for pride, what constitutes a title to esteem or praise — what can be displayed as a personal or collective accomplishment. Abraham would have a reason to boast if he had been justified by his works (Romans 4:2), but that is not the case.
4. The word also sometimes designates shared honor, the mutual pride that believers draw from one another: Paul tells the Corinthians that they are his glory, and vice versa (2 Corinthians 1:14).
G2745.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb for to boast or to glory. It literally designates that which one boasts about, the matter of boasting. In Hebrew, the ancient Bible often used words meaning praise or splendor for the same ideas. It is a noun that crystallizes the idea of founded or unfounded pride.
G2745.emploi: This word appears mainly in Paul’s epistles, about 11 times, particularly in his correspondence with the Corinthians and with the Galatians. Paul often uses it to question or correct: he asks whether a certain action truly offers a subject of glory, or he denounces misplaced glory. In Romans 4:2, he poses the question in principle (glorifying Abraham); in 1 Corinthians 5:6 and 9:15-16, he criticizes or refuses boasting. In 2 Corinthians, he broadens the meaning: the faithful can be the subject of glory for one another (1:14), or Paul gives the Corinthians something to boast about regarding him (5:12). It is a key word in Paul’s reflection on the legitimacy of Christian pride.
G2745.portee: This word invites an examination of the real foundation of our pride. The Bible acknowledges that it is possible to find glory in certain things — our faithfulness to the Gospel, our brothers and sisters in Christ — but it demands that this glory be just and heartfelt, not based on appearance or lies. For the Christian, it is an invitation to boast only in what is truly glorious before God.

sens: The act of boasting, of glorifying oneself about something
That of which one takes pride, what brings honor
The satisfaction of having accomplished something good
Blameworthy pride, vain boasting
G2746.detail:
1. In its primary sense, it is the act of glorifying oneself, of boasting publicly. In Romans 3:27, Paul excludes any "subject of boasting" before God by our works: faith alone justifies us, not our merits.
2. It is also the very thing one boasts about, that which makes us honorable. In 1 Thessalonians 2:19, Paul calls the Thessalonians his "crown of glory": they are his reason for pride before the Lord.
3. In a more positive usage, it is the rightful satisfaction of seeing good accomplished by others or by oneself. In 2 Corinthians 7:4, Paul "boasts" about his converts rightly: their faith is his comfort.
4. Finally, it is pride, blameworthy boasting. James 4:16 condemns this glorification as "vanity": it is contrary to the humility that God requires.
G2746.origine: The word comes from the verb καυχάομαι (to boast, to glorify oneself), which evokes the image of one who speaks loudly and proudly of their exploits. In Hebrew, it often translates תִּפְאָרָה (tifaret), which means "adornment," "ornament," "glory" — the idea that one adorns oneself with their accomplishments. The family of the word includes the verb "to glorify oneself" and the noun "subject of glory" (that which one boasts about).
G2746.emploi: This noun appears 12 times in the New Testament, mostly in Paul (Romans, 1 and 2 Corinthians, 1 Thessalonians) and once in James. Paul often uses it to reflect on spiritual pride: forbidden before God by our works alone (Romans 3:27), it is just towards others when it praises their faith (2 Corinthians 7:4, 8:24). In 2 Corinthians 11:10-11, he speaks of not being deprived of this "subject of glory": he is right to be proud of the Gospel he proclaims. James, on the other hand, outright rejects human boasting (James 4:16) as an ungodly presumption. The context thus determines whether glorification is commendable or blameworthy.
G2746.portee: This word teaches the Christian the crucial difference between two kinds of pride: that which boasts of oneself and one's merits, which God abhors, and that which rejoices in the good done by God in us and through us for Him, which is right and healthy. It calls for humility before the Lord, while allowing for sincere joy in God's work.

sens: eastern port of Corinth, Greece
place associated with Paul's departure to Syria
seat of an early Christian community
G2747.detail: Cenchreae is the maritime port of the city of Corinth, located to the east of the city on the Saronic Gulf. It is from there that Paul embarks to go to Syria after fulfilling a vow (Acts 18:18). This small port town also hosts a Christian community where Phoebe serves as a deaconess (Romans 16:1), showing that the Gospel had taken root even in the small ports of the Mediterranean basin.
G2747.origine: Cenchreae (in Greek Κεγχρεαί) is the Greek name of an ancient port attested in historical sources from the Roman period. The name likely comes from an ancient Greek root, although the exact etymology is uncertain. This specific geographical location is mentioned only in the New Testament in relation to Paul's apostolic activity.
G2747.emploi: Cenchreae appears twice in the New Testament, always in connection with Paul. In Acts 18:18, it is the port from which the apostle embarks after a stay in Corinth, highlighting its crucial role as a starting point for missionary journeys. In Romans 16:1, the mention of Phoebe as "deaconess of the church in Cenchreae" indicates that a Christian community was established there, significant enough to have recognized ministers. These two references attest to the strategic importance of this port for the early Christian movement in the Mediterranean.

sens: Stream that flows east of Jerusalem, between the city and the Mount of Olives
G2748.detail: 1. The Kidron is a watercourse, referred to as a "stream" in the Bible, which marks the eastern boundary of Jerusalem. It separates the city from the Mount of Olives, where Gethsemane is located. This stream only has water during the winter rains; the rest of the year, its bed remains dry.
G2748.origine: The Hebrew name קִדְרוֹן (Qidrôn) has an uncertain meaning. The Greeks of the New Testament transliterated it as Κεδρών (Kedron). This location appears already in the Old Testament, where it is mentioned as a territorial boundary and an important geographical landmark of Jerusalem.
G2748.emploi: The Kidron appears only once in the New Testament, in John 18:1. In this verse, Jesus and his disciples cross it after the last supper to go to Gethsemane, in a garden located on the other side of the stream. This passage marks the moment when Jesus leaves the place of the meal to enter into his passion.
G2748.portee: The crossing of the Kidron carries spiritual significance: it is by crossing this stream that Jesus separates from the rest of his disciples and enters into his redemptive passion. This concrete geographical detail anchors the central event of Christianity in history and in a specific location in Jerusalem.

sens: To be lying down, resting horizontally (for a person or a body)
To be placed, situated, located (for an object or thing)
To be intended, reserved, prepared for someone (figurative sense)
To be fixed, established, in effect (for a law or rule)
G2749.detail:
1. The verb first describes the physical state of one who is lying down. Mary and Joseph found the child Jesus "lying in the manger" (Luke 2:16): a natural position of rest. Similarly, after his crucifixion, the body of Jesus was "laid" in the tomb (Matthew 28:6, John 20:12), inert and lifeless. This is the image of the horizontal position, of forced or voluntary rest.
2. The verb then applies to objects: the water jars "lying" on the ground (John 20:5), the fish "lying" on the coals (John 21:9), the lamp that must not be "hidden under a bushel" (Matthew 5:14). It simply indicates where something is placed, situated, established.
3. Figuratively, the verb expresses what is set aside, reserved for the future. The rich man says: "You have many goods laid up for many years" (Luke 12:19) — goods "laid up", that is, set aside, stored. The idea is one of intended provision.
4. Finally, the verb can mean to be established, to be destined, to be fixed for a purpose. "You know that we are destined for this" (1 Thessalonians 3:3), meaning ordained, reserved for tribulations. The law is "established" for certain purposes (1 Timothy 1:9), laid down as a stable and unchanging foundation.
G2749.origine: The verb κεῖμαι (keimai) comes from an Indo-European root expressing the action of placing, laying down. It functions as the passive form of the verb τίθημι (titemi), which means "to place, to put". Κεῖμαι thus describes the resulting state: "to be placed, to be lying down, to remain in place". In Hebrew, it often translates verbs like יָעַד (yaad, "to designate") or forms of the verb "to sit, to rest". The word family includes compounds like ἀνάκειμαι ("to lie down, to recline at table") or ἐπίκειμαι ("to weigh upon, to be imposed"), which all retain the idea of stable position, of something that rests or is placed.
G2749.emploi: The verb appears 25 times in the New Testament, mostly in the Gospels and the epistles. In particular, Luke and John often describe physical position: the child in the manger, the body in the tomb, objects on the ground. In more abstract contexts, especially in Paul, it takes on an eschatological or legal sense: what is "laid down" is what is prepared, what is fixed, what awaits. In 1 John 5:19, "the whole world lies in wickedness" (κεῖται ἐν τῷ πονηρῷ) uses the verb metaphorically to express a state, an established and enduring condition. The religious context shows that κεῖμαι can qualify both a material and present reality (a body, a jar) and an invisible and future reality (a destined tribulation, a laid down sentence).
G2749.portee: This verb reminds us that certain things are not by chance: they are "laid down", "fixed", "destined". For the Christian, it sheds light on the mystery of divine providence — what God has ordained in advance. When Paul says that believers are "destined" for afflictions, he invites them not to passivity, but to trust: God has a plan, even in suffering. Moreover, κεῖμαι invites us to see the world as it is: not in agitated motion, but in apparent rest that hides a deeper reality. It is the verb of one who observes, who looks at things in their place — from the empty tomb to the law written on the heart.

sens: A tie or cord used to bind
A strip used to wrap a dead body
G2750.detail:
1. A band is a tie or cord that is wrapped around something to secure or hold it. The Greek word originally refers to a cord used in bedding (used to secure the mattress in ancient times).
2. Specifically, the bands are the strips that wrapped the body of a dead person before burial. This is the sense the word has in John 11:44, when the body of Lazarus comes out of the tomb "his feet and hands bound with strips" — these long linen strips that were wrapped around the corpse, a Jewish and Egyptian funerary practice.
G2750.origine: The Greek word κειρία comes from a root that evokes the idea of wrapping or binding. It is a common vocabulary word, used to refer to cords of all kinds: originally those that secured ancient beds, then by extension those that wrapped the dead. It is a popular term rather than a scholarly one, familiar to Greeks of the first century.
G2750.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in John 11:44, during the resurrection of Lazarus. Jesus commands the witnesses to "unbind" Lazarus from his bands, meaning to free his body from the strips that enveloped him according to Jewish funerary custom. This context shows that the bands were not just a simple shroud, but several layers of tightly wrapped fabric around the body.
G2750.portee: The scene at Lazarus' tomb reminds us that a physical covering — the bands, the linen — is only a hindrance when the new life of Christ has burst forth. Jesus commands to unbind the resurrected one: the meaning is clear for the Christian reader: resurrection frees from all that confines and paralyzes, and invites us to remove the veils that obscure the work of God.

sens: To cut short the hair or wool of a living creature
To remove the fleece from an animal (sheep, lamb)
To have one's hair cut or shaved (for oneself)
G2751.detail:
1. The verb κείρω means to cut short or shave hair, fur, or wool. It is the action of one who shears: he uses a sharp instrument to remove what grows. Acts 8:32 cites the prophet Isaiah speaking of a lamb led to the slaughter, silent like "a lamb silent before its shearer".
2. Applied to animals, the word mainly refers to the action of shearing the wool from a sheep or lamb. The context of Acts 8:32 evokes the lamb destined for sacrifice, defenseless before the one who shears it.
3. In the middle voice (when the subject acts upon himself), κείρω means to have one's hair cut or shaved. In 1 Corinthians 11:6, Paul speaks of a woman who cuts her hair; in Acts 18:18, Paul himself has his head shaved at Cenchreae after a vow he has taken.
G2751.origine: The verb κείρω comes from a root that expresses the action of cutting or slicing. In Hebrew, the same act is rendered by גָּזַז (gazaz), as in Isaiah 53:7 where the prophet speaks of the Servant of God led to sacrifice, silent like a lamb that is sheared. The middle form of the Greek verb indicates that the subject submits to this action or practices it on himself.
G2751.emploi: The verb κείρω appears only three times in the New Testament. Acts 8:32 cites it to translate Isaiah 53:7 in the account of the Ethiopian eunuch's conversion, where the gentleness of the sheared lamb symbolizes the gentleness of Christ led to death. Acts 18:18 mentions Paul shaving his head at Cenchreae to fulfill a vow (probably a Nazarite vow), an act marking the end of a religious undertaking. In 1 Corinthians 11:6, Paul discusses the appropriateness of cutting hair: a woman who rejects her veil must accept to be shorn, which is shameful according to the conventions of the time. These three uses share the idea of visible transformation and sometimes submission to a religious or cultural practice.
G2751.portee: This verb reminds us that our outward appearance and cultural practices can reflect our spiritual commitments or obedience to God. For Paul, shaving the head to fulfill a vow shows how concrete gestures of the body accompany the sincerity of faith. The citation of Isaiah 53:7 invites reflection on the gentleness and lack of resistance of Christ, the Lamb of God, led to death for our salvation.

sens: A cry, a command that orders or provokes an action
A call that is heard, notably from above to below
The moment when this order or call resonates
G2752.detail:
1. The word κέλευσμα primarily refers to a shouted command, an order given loudly to make someone act. It is the cry that says "Go!" or "Rise!" — a direct and imperative call. In 1 Thessalonians 4:16, it qualifies the signal given by the Lord himself at the return of Christ, a solemn order announcing the resurrection of the dead.
2. The word also evokes the idea of a voice descending, of an authority speaking from above. It is the call issued from a position of power — like a leader commanding their troops or the Lord commanding nature. This nuance of height and power colors the passage of the final judgment.
3. The word can designate the precise moment when this order resonates, the instant of the command. It is the point in time where the cry is heard and triggers a cascade of events.
G2752.origine: The word κέλευσμα comes from the verb κελεύω, which means "to order, command, shout an order." It is a noun formed from this verb to designate the action itself — the command as an event. The root carries the idea of a voice giving an order, often heard from afar and demanding quick obedience. The word is quite rare in the New Testament, and its presence in 1 Thessalonians 4:16 gives it an apocalyptic resonance.
G2752.emploi: The word κέλευσμα appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Thessalonians 4:16, where Paul describes the return of Christ. He chooses this term to emphasize that the resurrection of the dead will not be a silent or gradual event, but a manifest, audible command coming from the Lord himself — a signal that encompasses both the cry of the Lord, the voice of the archangel, and the sound of God's trumpet. This concentration of images (voice, cry, sound) makes κέλευσμα the decisive moment when the cosmic order changes and the dead rise.
G2752.portee: This word reminds the Christian that the return of Christ will not be a matter of doubt or ambiguity: it will be a command heard by all, a voice that breaks the silence of death and restores life. For those who await the Lord, it is a promise that this final call is certain, public, and irresistible — the divine signal that concludes history and opens eternity.

sens: To give a direct order to someone, with authority
To verbally communicate what is expected of someone
To implement a decision by command
G2753.detail:
1. To order is to give a command with authority: one addresses someone telling them to do something, and one expects to be obeyed. In Acts 4:15, the members of the Sanhedrin order the apostles Peter and John to leave the room to deliberate among themselves. It is an order given by one who has power.
2. The verb often emphasizes the spoken word, the act of commanding by voice rather than in writing or by gesture. In Matthew 18:25, the master verbally orders that his servant be sold to pay his debt: he pronounces this order in front of the servant or witnesses. It is the action of stating what must be done.
3. Sometimes to order means to execute a decision by communicating it to those who must carry it out. In Acts 22:30, the tribune orders the chief priests and the Sanhedrin to gather to question Paul: his command triggers an action. The word emphasizes less the decision itself than the act of conveying it with authority.
G2753.origine: The verb κελεύω comes from a root that evokes the idea of exhorting or pushing someone to act. It is fundamentally a communication verb: commanding is only possible through the word or gesture of one who has authority. In classical Greek, it describes the order given by a superior — a king, a general, a master — to one who must execute it. The family of the word is small in biblical Greek, but the verb is regularly used to translate the orders given by human authorities as well as by the Lord.
G2753.emploi: κελεύω appears 26 times in the New Testament, mostly in the Gospel of Matthew and in Acts. It almost always describes the order given by a recognized authority: a master to his servant (Matthew 18:25), a religious leader to his subordinates (Acts 4:15, 5:34), a magistrate or tribune to his soldiers (Acts 16:22, 22:30). Jesus also orders — to the crowd (Matthew 8:18) or to his disciples (Matthew 14:19, 27:64). The verb is rarely used kindly: most of the time, the one who orders exercises an objective authority over the one who obeys. It is a word of hierarchy and direct command.
G2753.portee: For the reader, this verb reminds us that authority is a real fact in the world: there are those who order and those who obey. When we see Jesus ordering, we recognize that he speaks from a place of sovereign authority. When we see human authorities ordering — often unjustly or cruelly — we understand that only God is the final judge of what must be done. It is a word that helps to see where true power resides.

sens: A desire for praise or honor devoid of real foundation
The pride of one who believes themselves superior without solid reason
A hollow pretense of greatness or merit
G2754.detail:
1. It is the hollow desire to appear glorious or esteemed in the eyes of others, without it being based on a reality or true virtue. In Philippians 2:3, Paul exhorts to do nothing "from vain glory": one must reject this thirst for admiration for what one is not truly.
2. It is the pride that leads one to believe themselves superior to others, to put oneself forward, without legitimate foundation. This attitude contrasts with the humility that Paul recommends in the same verse, which consists of "considering others as better than yourselves."
3. A hollow pretense: one who acts out of vain glory seeks the appearance of greatness rather than the reality of good or service. It is a self-centered motive that diverts action towards oneself rather than towards others or towards God.
G2754.origine: The Greek word comes from two roots: "keno" (empty, hollow) and "doxa" (glory, opinion, honor). It literally denotes a "empty glory." It is a rare compound word that describes an illusion of honor. The Greek adjective "kenodoxos" (vain) is the form from which this noun derives.
G2754.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Philippians 2:3. Paul uses it to warn against a motive for action that would be harmful to the unity and life of the local church. He directly opposes it to humility and consideration for others. This context shows that "vain glory" is a capital sin of the human heart, which arises from pride and selfishness.
G2754.portee: Recognizing vain glory in our actions compels us to honestly examine our motives: do we act to be seen, admired, or to build our reputation, or truly to serve others and honor God? Paul invites us to mortify it through humility and to place the interests of others before our own. It is an invitation to sincerity of heart in our Christian life.

sens: Pride that seeks to be valued by empty and unjustified glory
Arrogance that drives one to provoke and compete with others
Envy and jealousy fueled by the desire to be admired
G2755.detail:
1. Vain glory is that pride which chases after the esteem and praise of others, but has no solid foundation — it is glory that is worthless, hollow, and empty. When Paul warns the Galatians, "Let us not become conceited," he is specifically referring to this unhealthy desire to shine in the eyes of others, to be noticed and admired without valid reason (Galatians 5:26).
2. This vanity naturally leads to provocation and rivalry: one who wants to appear superior to others challenges and provokes them, seeking to surpass them. It is a poison for the life of the church, as one no longer seeks the common edification, but their own exaltation.
3. It breeds mutual envy and jealousy — the same envy spoken of in the following verses. When you see someone else admired, you covet their glory, and you are consumed by jealousy. It is a destructive cycle where each becomes the enemy of the other.
G2755.origine: The Greek word κενόδοξος (kenodoxos) is composed of two roots: κενός (kenos), which means "empty" or "without content," and δόξα (doxa), which means "glory" or "reputation." The basic image is that of a glory that is just wind, appearance without substance. It is a word that Paul invents or chooses to denounce an attitude that has absolutely no spiritual solidity: seeking to shine for the pleasure of shining, nothing more.
G2755.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Galatians 5:26, where Paul uses it in his exhortation to the Christians in Galatia. It is part of a list of warnings against behaviors that destroy the community and testify to a carnal, not spiritual, walk. Paul places this vice alongside mutual provocation and envy: it is a characteristic attitude of the flesh, of our unregenerate nature, which wants to dominate, appear, and crush others.
G2755.portee: For today's Christian, this word is a merciless mirror. How many times do we seek to impress, to be recognized, to surpass others in our church or our work? Vain glory is the discreet poison of the Christian life, because it can hide under respectable clothing. Paul reminds us that this quest for empty esteem distances us from love for our neighbor and humility. It is a call to question ourselves: do we act for the glory of God, or for our own glory?

sens: That is empty, devoid of content
That has no result, effect, or efficacy
That is lacking in foundation, truth, or usefulness
That lacks wisdom, sense, or moral value
G2756.detail:
1. The primary meaning is literally empty: a container with nothing inside, a hand that bears nothing. Mark 12:3 shows a servant sent back "empty" of any gift for his master, hands without offering. It is the image of physical absence.

2. Figuratively, vain describes what leads to nothing, what remains ineffective despite the efforts invested. A vain preaching (1 Corinthians 15:14) has not transformed those who heard it; a vain work (1 Corinthians 15:58) bears no fruit.

3. The word also qualifies what is hollow in foundation and truth: vain speeches (Ephesians 5:6) are seductive but deceptive words, lacking solidity. It is a deception that seduces without enlightening.

4. Applied to people, vain means devoid of true wisdom, living in illusion. James 2:20 speaks of a "vain" faith, meaning emptied of its living and active content — a dead, ineffective belief.
G2756.origine: The word comes from a root that evokes emptiness, the absence of substance. In Hebrew, it corresponds mainly to "רִיק" (rîq), which literally means empty. The basic image is that of nothingness, of what is not filled. The family of kenos also includes the noun "kenodoxia" (vanity, vain pride) and "kenwsis" (the emptying of Christ, literally his emptying of glory).
G2756.emploi: The word appears 16 times in the New Testament, mostly in Paul. In the concrete sense, it describes empty hands: a mistreated servant sent away without pay (Mark 12:3, Luke 20:10). In the figurative sense, it abounds in Paul's epistles. Paul uses it to warn against hollow words (Ephesians 5:6), against false wisdom (Colossians 2:8), and especially to defend the reality of Christ's resurrection: if it did not happen, our faith and preaching are completely vain (1 Corinthians 15:14). The expression "in vain" (eis kenon) appears several times to exhort: do not receive the grace of God in vain (2 Corinthians 6:1), do not labor in vain for the Lord.
G2756.portee: For the Christian reader, this word exposes the danger of emptiness: a faith without solid foundation, words that seduce without transforming, a life of labor without anchoring in Christ. Paul uses it to stimulate perseverance and vigilance: refusing the vain means seeking substance, truth that has weight and produces lasting fruit. It is a call to authenticity in faith and in the service of God.

sens: Hollow word, without foundation, that sounds empty
Speech delivered without reflection, sterile chatter
False or deceptive teaching that leads away from the truth
G2757.detail:
1. A vain discourse is a hollow word that contains nothing solid: it resonates like an empty noise, it makes noise but brings nothing. That is why Paul exhorts Timothy to guard the deposit of faith "by avoiding vain and profane babble" (1 Timothy 6:20): it is not just about useless words, but about words that empty faith of its content.
2. It is also thoughtless chatter, words thrown to the wind without reflection or depth. This type of language characterizes those who "will proceed further in ungodliness" (2 Timothy 2:16), as if each light word distances them further from God.
3. The word also encompasses false teachings that deceive: these vain discourses are "profane," they pollute the purity of the Gospel. Their effect is destructive, "will eat like gangrene" (2 Timothy 2:16), contaminating the faith of the listeners.
G2757.origine: The Greek word κενοφωνία is composed of κενός ("empty, hollow") and φωνή ("voice, word"). It literally means "empty voice." The root κενός evokes the absence of substance, nothingness; it belongs to the same family as κενολογέω ("to speak vainly"), which translates the Hebrew צָפַף used in Isaiah 8:19 to describe the sterile chatter of mediums and diviners who consult only the dead.
G2757.emploi: This word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in the pastoral epistles addressed to Timothy. In 1 Timothy 6:20, Paul commands his disciple to "guard the deposit" by fleeing from vain and profane discourses: these are heterodox doctrines that were already circulating in the early Church and threatening the purity of apostolic teaching. In 2 Timothy 2:16, the exhortation is even more serious: those who hold such discourses advance "further in ungodliness" and their word spreads like gangrene. Paul thus emphasizes the progressive and contagious danger of vain discourse: it must not only be avoided but actively prohibited to protect the community.
G2757.portee: For the Christian, this word warns us against the allure of beautiful speech that says nothing, of brilliant but hollow discourse, and even more against teachings that distort the faith. It calls us to vigilance: even then, ungodliness was progressing "by word" (2 Timothy 2:16). This invites us to discern the spiritual value of what we listen to, read, and say ourselves, and to refuse to turn faith into sterile chatter or intellectual entertainment.

sens: Make empty, remove the contents
Render null, ineffective, devoid of value
Reduce to nothing, annihilate
Deprive oneself, empty oneself of something
G2758.detail:
1. Literally, the word means to make empty by removing what fills. This is the basic image: emptying a container, a place. Although this primary meaning is not illustrated in the provided texts, it underlies all figurative uses.

2. Figuratively, "empty" means to render ineffective, devoid of force or value. Faith becomes vain (Romans 4:14) when it loses its real significance — it is emptied of its living content. Similarly, proclaiming the Gospel with the wisdom of language risks rendering the cross of Christ vain (1 Corinthians 1:17), weakening its inherent power.

3. The word also denotes the action of reducing to nothing, of removing. When Paul asks God not to annihilate his subject of glory (1 Corinthians 9:15), he fears that it may be emptied, eliminated, reduced to nothing.

4. Philippians 2:7 presents the strongest and most personal use: Christ "emptied himself." He emptied himself of his glory, of his equality with God, by taking the form of a mere servant. This is a voluntary act of self-humbling.
G2758.origine: The word comes from the adjective "kenós" which means "empty." The root evokes the idea of a space devoid of content, of substance. In Hebrew, the corresponding verb often translated by this term in the Greek version of the Old Testament is related to the idea of loss and vanity. The figurative use of the word — to render vain, to annihilate — naturally extends the concrete meaning: to empty something of its value, its effectiveness, its reason for being.
G2758.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the New Testament, always in the writings of the Apostle Paul. In Romans 4:14 and 1 Corinthians 1:17, it means "to render vain," "to deprive of effect." In 1 Corinthians 9:15, it describes the action of removing, of eliminating. The most famous and profound use is Philippians 2:7, where Paul describes the incarnation of Christ: the Son of God voluntarily emptied himself of his glory to take the form of a servant. This passage places the word at the heart of the mystery of the incarnation and the sacrifice of Christ. In all these contexts, the word carries a strong theological weight: it is never a simple disappearance, but an active cancellation, an action that deprives something of its power or value.
G2758.portee: This word challenges the Christian regarding the reality of Christ's work and the nature of the divine sacrifice. In Philippians 2:7, Christ's self-humbling is the ultimate model of obedience and love: the Lord voluntarily emptied himself for our salvation. The word also reminds us that the power of the Gospel and the cross remains intact when proclaimed straightforwardly. It is a call to transparency and faithfulness in the proclamation of faith.

sens: Sharp point or thorn that stings and wounds
Pointed instrument used to prick animals to make them move
The cause of death or suffering
That which provokes revolt or resistance
G2759.detail: 1. The sting is primarily a sharp point that stings: in Revelation 9:10, the apocalyptic locusts have stings in their tails, weapons of combat. 2. It is also a pointed stick or goad used to prick draft animals, especially oxen, to direct or force them to move — hence the expression "kick against the goads" (Acts 26:14), which means "to resist vainly a force that dominates you," like a beast kicking against the goad that hurts it. 3. Figuratively, the sting becomes what causes death or suffering: in 1 Corinthians 15:56, "the sting of death is sin," meaning that sin is what gives death its deadly power. 4. More broadly, it is what pricks the conscience or provokes revolt: when Jesus says to Saul, "it is hard for you to kick against the goads" (Acts 9:5), he means that persecuting Jesus is rebelling against an invincible force that will ultimately hurt you.
G2759.origine: The Greek word kentron comes from a root meaning "to prick" or "to pierce." In Hebrew, it corresponds to several words for what pricks or wounds: the bit, the sting, or even the thorn. The same Greek word can refer to both the combat weapon of an insect and an agricultural instrument or, figuratively, the cause of spiritual suffering.
G2759.emploi: This word appears 5 times in the New Testament, always in the sense of sting. In Revelation 9:10, it refers to the stinger of the locusts of plague. In Acts 9:5 and 26:14, it is a figurative sting: Jesus rebukes Saul by saying that it is useless to resist God, like an ox that "kicks" against the goad that pricks it. In 1 Corinthians 15:55-56, Paul uses it twice in his meditation on victory over death: first as an image of death itself ("O death, where is your sting?"), then as the secret power of sin that makes death deadly. In all cases, the stinging evokes a force that imposes itself irresistibly.
G2759.portee: This word reminds us that sin wounds deeply like a sting and that death has a formidable power because it is linked to sin. But it also tells us that our resistance to God is vain, like the rebellion of the ox against the goad: Christ's victory over death has removed its sting, and the believer can cry out, "O death, where is your sting?" by trusting in the resurrection.

sens: Roman officer commanding a unit of one hundred soldiers
The high-ranking Roman soldier who exercises direct authority over his men
G2760.detail:
1. A centurion is an officer in the Roman army who commands about one hundred soldiers (the word comes from the Latin "centurio"). He is a trusted man, often recruited for his experience and valor in battle. In Mark 15:39, the centurion who guarded Jesus at the cross witnesses his death and draws a profound spiritual conclusion: "Truly, this man was the Son of God."
2. The centurion is also a representative of Roman power, tasked with executing the orders of his superiors. Pilate consults him (Mark 15:44-45) to confirm that Jesus is truly dead, as the centurion, by his position, is the best person to know for certain.
G2760.origine: The Greek word κεντυρίων is a direct borrowing from the Latin centurio, which literally means "one who commands a hundred." The Latin root centum means "hundred." Although Mark uses this direct Latin term, Matthew and Luke prefer to use ἑκατόνταρχος (hekaton-tarkhos), composed of the Greek ἑκατόν (hundred) and ἀρχ- (to command), which means exactly the same thing but with an entirely Greek formation.
G2760.emploi: The word appears only three times, all in the Gospel of Mark at the time of Jesus' crucifixion (Mark 15:39, 44, 45). Mark chooses the more direct Latin term, while Matthew and Luke, elsewhere in the Gospels, prefer the Greek compound. The centurion in Mark 15 plays a key role: as a witness to Jesus' death, he is the first to confess his divinity, and it is with him that Pilate verifies the death before handing the body over to Joseph of Arimathea.
G2760.portee: The Roman centurion, taken as a witness of the crucifixion, becomes the spokesperson for a crucial truth: Jesus is the Son of God. Mark emphasizes that this major confession does not come from a disciple or an Israelite believer, but from a representative of the power that crucified him. It is an invitation to see in Jesus' death not a mere political event, but a divine event that transcends boundaries and converts hearts.

sens: Without result, without effect
Without foundation, without valid reason
In a futile or sterile manner
G2761.detail:
1. The word describes an action that does not lead to anything, that produces no fruit. When it is said that a word is spoken "in vain," it means that it does not fulfill its role, that it remains empty of meaning or effectiveness — exactly like a nutshell without a kernel. In James 4:5, the apostle questions: "Do you think that the Scripture speaks in vain?" meaning: "Do you think that holy words would remain without effect or significance?"
2. The word also evokes the absence of foundation or justification. It is an action done without serious reason, without real purpose. This can qualify a hollow word, a promise that one never intends to keep, or a worry without true cause.
3. In a broader sense, the word suggests vanity, futility — that which is hollow, which does not deserve concern, which produces nothing lasting.
G2761.origine: The Greek word κενῶς (kenōs) comes from the adjective κενός (kenos), which means "empty," "hollow." This root evokes the image of a container without content, hence the idea that something is devoid of effect or meaning. In the Greek Old Testament, this word often translates the Hebrew רִיק (rîq), which has the same force: empty, without result. The adverb "in vain" thus expresses the transition from spatial emptiness to emptiness of effectiveness.
G2761.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in James 4:5. James uses it in a theological argument: he defends the authority of Holy Scripture by asking his readers if they can really believe that it would speak without effect or relevance. The context shows that the apostle contrasts the apparent sterility of vain words with the living power of the divine word that dwells in us. It is a call not to take lightly what God has said.
G2761.portee: This word reminds us that every word counts, especially God's. It does not fall empty or without fruit. For the Christian, this means that praying, interceding, or confessing God's Word is never a waste of time: God hears and responds. Conversely, the word invites us to examine our own words — do we speak with a real aim, or do we let hollow and purposeless words come out of our mouths?

sens: Small graphic detail that distinguishes certain Hebrew letters from one another
G2762.detail: 1. It is a small extension or point that changes the shape of a Hebrew letter — for example, the stroke that transforms the letter ד (dalet) into ר (rech). The word literally means "small horn" due to this pointed aspect. Jesus uses it in Matthew 5:18 to emphasize that every minute detail of the Mosaic Law, even in its writing, has permanent value: "Not one jot or one letter stroke will pass from the law." What is so small that one might forget or neglect will remain until all things are fulfilled.
G2762.origine: The word comes from a root that means "horn" or "point." Its basic image — that of a small sharp protrusion — perfectly applies to the fine detail that visually distinguishes two characters of writing. In Hebrew, these small distinguishing elements were well known to the scribes who copied the Law.
G2762.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in the context of Jesus' teaching on the permanence and authority of the Law. In Matthew 5:18, it comes immediately after "jot" (the smallest Hebrew letter), forming a pair: Jesus means that not only will no letter disappear, but also no minute detail of a letter will pass away. The same assertion appears in Luke 16:17, in the context of the Sermon on the Mount. Both passages use this term to express the immutability and absolute importance of every element of divine Law.
G2762.portee: This word invites the reader to be aware of the extreme attention that Jesus pays to the Word of God and its inviolability. It teaches that nothing, not even what is tiny or easily ignored, escapes God's eyes or the value He places on His Law. For Christian life, this underscores that our respect for the biblical Word must be scrupulous and that God honors those who take it seriously in every detail.

sens: artisan who shapes clay to make vessels
one who has absolute authority over his material, who can dispose of it at will
G2763G.detail:
1. The potter is the artisan who works with clay: he kneads it, shapes it on his wheel, and fires it to make vessels used to hold or transport water, oil, or wine. It is an ancient and common trade in Palestine and the Mediterranean.
2. Figuratively, the potter becomes the image of the creator who shapes his creation according to his will. Paul uses it in Romans 9:21: "Does not the potter have power over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?" This comparison illustrates God's sovereign power over His creatures, just as a potter freely disposes of his material without accounting to the clay.
G2763G.origine: The Greek word comes from a root that evokes mixing and preparation. In Hebrew, Psalm 2:9 and Jeremiah 18:2 use a word (יָצַר, yatsar) that means "to form, to shape" and also refers to the potter; the Septuagint, the Greek version of the Old Testament, translated it with this term to show that the same God who shaped the clay in the past continues to shape the history of His people.
G2763G.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Romans 9:21, in a parable where Paul exposes God's right to dispose of nations and individuals according to His sovereign will. The context is that of predestination: God freely chooses whom He will save and whom He will harden, just as a potter freely chooses whether the clay will be made into a prestigious vessel or an ordinary one. This image is rooted in the prophetic tradition of the Old Testament, where God often compares Himself to the potter who remakes Israel.
G2763G.portee: This image of the potter reminds the believer that God has absolute authority and wisdom over our lives. It invites humility: we are not the masters of our destiny, but the material in the hands of the Creator. At the same time, it affirms that this sovereignty is never arbitrary or unjust, as it emanates from infinite wisdom and justice. For the reader, it is an invitation to trust in God rather than to rebel against Him.

sens: artisan who shapes clay to make vases and dishes
one who works the earth, an image of divine creative power
G2763H.detail:
1. A potter is an artisan who takes raw clay and molds it to create vases, pots, and dishes. It is an ancient profession, well-known in Palestine. In Matthew 27:7, after the death of Jesus, the leaders buy "the potter's field" with the thirty pieces of silver, a land that likely belonged to a potter or was used to extract clay.
2. In the Bible, the potter becomes a powerful image of God the creator. Just as the potter shapes the clay according to his will, God shapes creatures and nations according to His plan (Romans 9:21). This connection also appears in the Old Testament with the prophets: Jeremiah visits a potter to understand how God "remakes" the peoples (Jeremiah 18:2 in the Greek translation).
G2763H.origine: The Greek word kerameus comes from kerannumi (to mix, to prepare), as the potter prepares and mixes the clay before shaping it. In Hebrew, we find yatsar (יָצַר), which literally means "to form, to shape" — the same verb used to describe how God formed man from the dust (Genesis 2:7). The context of creation closely links the human potter to the divine act of creation.
G2763H.emploi: The word appears twice in the Segond, both in Matthew 27, to refer to the "potter's field." This field was a cemetery where foreigners and the poor were buried, purchased with the rejected money of Judas. This place will become known as "the Field of Blood" according to Acts 1:19. Beyond this historical context, the potter symbolizes elsewhere in the Bible (notably in Romans 9:21) divine sovereignty: God is the potter, we are the clay, and He shapes us according to His will.
G2763H.portee: Meditating on the image of the potter reminds the Christian that God is the sovereign creator who shapes our lives according to His design. This invites humility: we are merely clay in the hands of the divine potter. This image, far from being overwhelming, can also reassure the believer: our lives have a form and meaning intended by the One who created us.

sens: Made of clay, earthenware
Fragile, of little value, destined to be broken
G2764.detail:
1. This word simply describes what is made of clay or earthenware — the raw material that the potter shapes. In Revelation 2:27, "the vessels of clay" refer to ordinary, worthless containers that can be easily broken.
2. By extension, the word takes on a symbolic meaning: clay evokes fragility. These clay vessels represent what is perishable, what breaks easily. The image of the king who "breaks the clay vessels" expresses absolute power over what is weak and defenseless.
G2764.origine: The word comes from κέραμος (keramos, pottery), which designates clay or the work of the potter. In Hebrew, the Greek Old Testament uses this word to translate פֶּחָר (péḥar, clay). The family of the word κέραμος evokes the work of the potter: one who shapes clay to make utensils.
G2764.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Revelation 2:27. In the apocalyptic context, Jesus promises the victor the power to "shepherd the nations with a rod of iron" and to "break them as one breaks the clay vessels." The word emphasizes the opposition between the fragility of earthly vessels (sinful humanity or the powers of the world) and the strength of the one who reigns. This image recalls the Old Testament and the biblical idea of the potter and the clay.
G2764.portee: This word invites the believer to see their own fragility before God — we are clay in the hands of the Creator. At the same time, Revelation 2:27 affirms that those who believe in Christ will receive authority over what seems insurmountable: the clay vessels, as fragile as they may be, will be broken by the power of His word.

sens: earthenware container for drawing and transporting water
symbol of humble and discreet service
G2765.detail:
1. A pitcher is an earthenware container, elongated in shape with a handle, used for drawing and transporting water or other liquids. It is a common object in daily life in Palestine, familiar to every family. In the two parallel accounts of the Passion (Mark 14:13 and Luke 22:10), Jesus sends His disciples "to the city": they will recognize the master of the house by this sign: "you will meet a man carrying a pitcher of water."
2. Beyond the concrete object, the pitcher becomes in these passages a symbol of silent service and availability. The one who carries the water does not perform a glorious task, but a humble one — this is precisely why this detail allows the disciples to identify the place: in a culture where women usually carried water, a man carrying a pitcher was a remarkable sign of dedication.
G2765.origine: The Greek word keramion comes from keramos, which means "clay" or "earthenware." It is a diminutive, indicating an object shaped from earth: a "small thing of earth." The same root has given rise to "ceramic" in modern French. In Hebrew, the word גְּבִיעַ (gubia) also designates a container, often translated as "cup" or "vessel," and appears notably in Jeremiah 35:5. The word keramion emphasizes the material — the earth — rather than the precise shape.
G2765.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in the accounts of the preparation for Passover before the Passion: Mark 14:13 and Luke 22:10. In both cases, a pitcher of water is the detail that allows the disciples to identify the master of the house who will welcome them for the Passover meal. This concrete and picturesque detail anchors the narrative in Palestinian reality. The meaning remains constant: it is always a material, concrete object filled with water.
G2765.portee: This word reminds us that the Gospels are rooted in a concrete historical reality: the small details of daily life (a pitcher, a man carrying it) testify that the accounts of Jesus are not abstract legends, but stories that took place in a real time and place. For the disciple of Jesus, this image of the one who carries the water also speaks of humility and availability for service.

sens: material used to make pottery and tiles, clay
terracotta container
terracotta roofing element placed on a roof
G2766.detail:
1. The word κέραμος primarily refers to clay, the earth from which potters shape their objects. It is the raw, malleable, and common material found in nature that is fired to harden it.
2. It can then refer to any object shaped from this clay: a jar, a pot, a pitcher. It is the finished product of the potter's work.
3. Finally, in antiquity, the word particularly applies to roof tiles, these terracotta slabs that, when assembled together, form the covering of houses. This last meaning is illustrated in Luke 5:19, where the friends of the paralyzed man break through the roof to lower him down to Jesus: they remove the tiles to create an opening through which to pass the sick man on his bed.
G2766.origine: The word comes from the verb κεράννυμι (‘to mix’), since the clay was prepared by mixing earth with water. The root thus evokes the fundamental work of the potter: to mix, knead the raw material to make it moldable. The word is attested in ancient Greek to refer to both the material and the finished product, reflecting a very everyday reality: most household items, from clothing to cooking to construction, used ceramics.
G2766.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 5:19. In this famous passage, the four friends who want to bring a paralyzed man to Jesus cannot find an entrance due to the crowd; they then go up on the roof and remove the tiles to create a sufficiently large opening. This detail shows how the houses of Galilee had roofs made of terracotta tiles, which could be removed without demolishing the entire structure. The action carries a spiritual significance: these men demonstrate their faith and ingenuity to bring the sick man to Jesus, and the Lord rewards their perseverance.
G2766.portee: This mention of tiles immerses us in the concrete context of daily life in Galilee in the first century. It also shows the determination of those seeking to meet Jesus: beyond material obstacles and the crowd, their faith drives them to act boldly. For the Christian reader, the image of the roof from which tiles are removed becomes a symbol of the energy and creativity that faith requires: sometimes one must circumvent obstacles through unexpected means to reach Jesus.

sens: Hard bony projection that comes from the head of certain animals
Small projections at the corner of an altar
Symbol of strength, power, or authority
Representation of a political power or kingdom
G2768.detail:
1. The horn is a natural growth that some animals have, such as rams or goats. In Revelation 13:11, the beast ‘had two horns like a lamb,’ which describes a recognizable physical trait.
2. The golden altar had small horns at its four corners, where the blood of sacrifices was poured (Revelation 9:13 mentions ‘the four horns of the golden altar’).
3. A horn represents the power or strength of a person: in Luke 1:69, ‘horn of salvation’ means a powerful Savior, capable of delivering us.
4. In the visions of Revelation, horns symbolize kingdoms or political powers. A dragon or beast with ten horns (Revelation 12:3, 13:1) represents a power that dominates through ten kings or ten kingdoms.
G2768.origine: The Greek word κέρας comes from an ancient root meaning the natural horn of animals. In Hebrew, the word קָרַן (karan) has the same meaning, and Greek translators used it to render this term in the Old Testament. The horn naturally evokes a weapon or instrument of power — which has made the word a natural symbol of strength in biblical language.
G2768.emploi: The word appears ten times in biblical Greek, almost all in Revelation. It first refers to the physical horn of the altar (Revelation 9:13) and the traits of visionary beasts (Revelation 5:6, 12:3, 13:1, 13:11, 17:3, 17:7, 17:12, 17:16). Only once, in Luke 1:69, is it used figuratively for power: ‘horn of salvation’ is a poetic expression for a strong Savior. In apocalyptic visions, the number of horns varies (seven, ten, two) and each horn represents a distinct power or kingdom.
G2768.portee: For the Christian, the word ‘horn’ in Revelation reminds us that earthly powers, however terrifying they may seem, remain under God's control. In Luke 1:69, it testifies to the strength and majesty of the promised Savior: Jesus is not a weak Messiah, but powerful to save us. The word invites the reader not to fear human authorities, but to recognize the supremacy of Christ.

sens: Fruit of the shrub called carob tree
Long, brown pod filled with sweet pulp and hard seeds
Poor food given to animals, symbol of extreme poverty
G2769.detail:
1. The carob is the fruit of the carob tree, a shrub that grows in Mediterranean regions. It is a long, dark brown pod containing sweet pulp and hard seeds.
2. This fruit was common in Palestine: it was given to pigs for feeding, as shown in the parable of the prodigal son (Luke 15:16). It was cheap food, hardly fit for a man.
3. By extension, the word symbolizes degradation and absolute lack: the prodigal son, reduced to misery, comes to envy the food of the animals—a detail that underscores the humiliation of his state.
G2769.origine: The Greek word κεράτιον comes from κέρας ("horn"), as the pod resembles a small horn. It is a diminutive affectionate or descriptive term from ancient Greek. The carob was well known in the Greek and Roman world as food for livestock.
G2769.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 15:16, in the parable of the prodigal son. It is a concrete and striking detail: at the moment of his greatest misery, the hungry young man would have liked to eat the carobs that the pigs consumed. This detail shows the extreme poverty and humiliation of the character, much more than the simple lack of food. The use of the word highlights the contrast between his past wealth and his present destitution.
G2769.portee: The mention of carobs in the parable of the prodigal son speaks to the heart of the reader. It shows that spiritual misery—the separation from the Father—is worse than physical hunger. It is by reaching this depth of humiliation that the prodigal son awakens and returns. For us, this word reminds us that extreme circumstances can be a grace that brings us back to God.

sens: Obtain a profit, a material or financial advantage
Win, reap a benefit in business or in a project
Conquer, attract to oneself, win someone's adherence
Avoid, escape from danger or harm
Acquire something instead of losing something else
G2770.detail:
1. Obtain a profit or a material or financial advantage: this is primarily the commercial, concrete sense. The servant who "gains" five talents (Matthew 25:16) has made them grow, multiplied through work. It is the image of the merchant who does his accounts and sees his money increase.

2. Win, reap a benefit in business or project: to gain also means to profit from a situation or action. James 4:13 mentions merchants who plan to "gain," meaning to conduct profitable trade. It is to produce something of value and benefit from it.

3. Conquer, attract to oneself, win someone's adherence: when Paul says "I gain the Jews" (1 Corinthians 9:20), he is not talking about money but about people. It is to win a person to faith, to attract, to convert—like conquering an ally. In Matthew 18:15, gaining the brother who has sinned means bringing him back to God.

4. Avoid, escape from danger or harm: in Acts 27:21, "avoid this peril" is a nuance of the verb. Gaining safety means sparing oneself from harm, fleeing damage. The same verb can thus mean "not to lose" in the sense of "to protect oneself."

5. Acquire something instead of losing something else: this is the heart of Jesus' message in Matthew 16:26. Gaining the whole world but losing one's soul—the expression raises the question: what is true profit? What is called "gain" in the world (wealth, prestige) can be a total loss before God.
G2770.origine: The verb κερδαίνω comes from an Indo-European root related to the idea of "profit" or "advantage." In Greek, the noun κέρδος (kerdos) means "gain" or "profit" and gives rise to this verb. The basic image is that of commerce: to accumulate, increase, make prosper. In the Greek Bible of the Old Testament, this verb often translates the Hebrew idea of benefit or profitable cunning. It is a word from the concrete language of the market and exchange.
G2770.emploi: The verb κερδαίνω appears 16 times in the New Testament, especially in Matthew, who is particularly interested in it (Matthew 16:26, 18:15, 25:16-17 and 25:20-22). It primarily denotes an economic gain: the servants in Matthew 25 "gain" talents by investing them. This is the task of the good steward. But very quickly the verb enriches in meaning: to gain a person (1 Corinthians 9:19-22) is to convert or attract them to faith—this is the heart of Paul's mission. Finally, Jesus uses it critically in Matthew 16:26 and Mark 8:36: "gaining the world" but losing one's soul is a false profit, a catastrophic loss. Acts 27:21 shows the nuance of "avoiding": not suffering damage is also a form of gain.
G2770.portee: This word invites the believer to redefine what he considers true profit. Jesus turns the common meaning of the word upside down: in the world, one believes to gain by accumulating goods, prestige, power. But Jesus asks: what profit does a man have if he gains the whole world but loses his soul? The Christian faith measures gain by a different scale of values. At the same time, Paul speaks of "gaining" souls for Christ—this too is a profit, but in a renewed, spiritual sense. For the believer, it is to relearn to calculate: what is truly worth it? What should I seek to gain, and at what cost?

sens: Material profit, financial advantage
Benefit or advantage of any kind
Precious acquisition, what one gains in value
G2771.detail:
1. Material profit, financial advantage: the word primarily refers to the money one earns, the benefit derived from a business. In Titus 1:11, false teachers teach "for shameful gain": they seek to enrich themselves by deceiving people.
2. Benefit or advantage of any kind: the word extends to anything that advantages, enriches, or profits, in a broad sense. Paul says in Philippians 3:7 that he has considered as loss "the things that were gains for me"—everything that made him proud or prosperous in his past life without Christ.
3. Precious acquisition, what one gains in value: the word can refer to what is deeply profitable for us. In Philippians 1:21, "to die is gain"—to die is to gain something infinitely precious, the eternal presence of Christ.
G2771.origine: The Greek word κέρδος comes from an Indo-European root that expresses the idea of profit and advantage. The word belongs to the family of verbs meaning "to gain, to profit." In the Greek Old Testament, it sometimes translates Hebrew words denoting profit or material advantage. The word is simple and direct, without intrinsic moral connotation: it is the usage that imbues it with positive or negative meaning.
G2771.emploi: The word κέρδος appears three times in the New Testament, all in Paul's epistles. In Philippians 1:21, it takes on a profound spiritual significance: for Paul, death is a true gain, far more precious than earthly life. In Philippians 3:7, Paul lists the human and religious advantages he possessed—prestige, wealth, status—and calls them "gains" that he has now renounced considering as precious. In Titus 1:11, the word takes on a negative connotation: material gain becomes the idol that drives false teachers to teach false doctrine. Thus, the word remains neutral, but faith reveals what is truly profitable.
G2771.portee: This word invites the Christian to reflect on what he truly considers gain. For Paul, nothing compares to Christ: death itself becomes gain if it brings us closer to Him. Money and human advantages are a true gain only if they serve the Gospel; pursued for their own sake, they become a loss. The Christian is called to evaluate his life, ambitions, and acquisitions in light of his relationship with Christ, and to discern authentic gain from deceptive gain.

sens: Small metal coin used as money
Small change, coins of little value
G2772.detail:
1. The word refers to a coin, a small metal piece minted for exchanges and payments. It is money in a concrete sense, something that can be held in one's hand. In John 2:15, Jesus "scattered the currency of the money changers": this refers to the coins that merchants had accumulated by exchanging the money of pilgrims for temple coins.
2. The word emphasizes the small, fragmented nature of this currency: these are not large sums, but small coins, change. This is why the text uses the plural: coins scattered here and there when Jesus overturned the tables.
G2772.origine: The word comes from a Greek root meaning "to cut," "to slice" (hence also "scissors"). Originally, a coin was indeed a piece of metal cut and stamped with an official seal. The word has retained this notion of a small portion, a fragment.
G2772.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in John 2:15, during the account of Jesus driving the merchants out of the temple. It specifically refers to the currency that the money changers had accumulated by exchanging the currencies of pilgrims who came from everywhere for worship. This detail paints the scene: amidst the chaos created by Jesus, the coins scatter on the temple floor, symbolizing the disorder brought by the Lord's judgment.
G2772.portee: This word reminds us that Jesus did not tolerate profane commerce invading the holy place. The detail of the scattered currency illustrates how radical and uncompromising the purification of the temple was: the money that polluted worship had to be scattered and lost. It is a call to purity of heart in our worship.
